introduction-the-pick-any-two-reality.core: With finite people, money and time, you can't maximise velocity, reliability and cost efficiency at once. Improving one almost always costs another.

first_principles.problem: Leaders ask for features faster, fewer outages and a smaller bill, all at the same time. Without naming the trade-off, teams quietly sacrifice whichever side isn't measured, usually reliability.
truths: Reliability work competes with feature work.
Money can buy speed or safety, but it's limited too.
derivation: Name the three vertices: **velocity, reliability, cost**.
Accept you can **optimise two at the expense of the third**.
Make the sacrifice **explicit**, not accidental.

analogy.title: A kitchen renovation
analogy.story: Fast, beautiful, cheap: pick two. Rushed and cheap means crooked tiles; beautiful and fast means a huge bill.
analogy.breaks: A renovation ends. Software keeps running, so the sacrificed side keeps charging interest.

example.title: "All three, please"
example.scenario: A product lead asks for a big launch in 2 weeks, no extra budget, zero incidents.

steps.label: Explicit
steps.detail: "With this timeline and budget we accept higher incident risk", or move the date.

example.outcome: trade-offs are decided by leaders, not discovered in production.

check.q: What happens if the trade-off isn't named?
check.a: The least-measured side, usually reliability, gets sacrificed silently.

defining-the-three-constraints.core: Each vertex needs a measurable definition: velocity by DORA metrics, reliability by SLOs and incident data, and cost by fully-loaded spend (people, infrastructure, tools, opportunity).

first_principles.problem: "We need to go faster" or "be more reliable" can't be traded off if nobody can measure them. Vague goals lead to vague decisions.
truths: Headcount is usually the biggest cost.
derivation: **Velocity**: deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, time to restore (DORA).
**Reliability**: SLO attainment, incidents, MTTR, error budget.
**Cost**: cloud bill + people + tools + opportunity cost.

analogy.title: A car dashboard
analogy.story: Speed, fuel and engine temperature each have a gauge. You can't trade speed for fuel economy if you can't see either.
analogy.breaks: Car gauges are built in. Engineering metrics must be deliberately instrumented.

example.title: A team that 'ships a lot'
example.scenario: 50 PRs merged per week but one monthly release.

steps.label: Measure
steps.detail: Lead time is 3 weeks from commit to production.

steps.label: Insight
steps.detail: The bottleneck is the release train, not coding.

check.a: Deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, and time to restore service.

the-trade-off-dynamics.core: Each pairing has a predictable sacrifice: fast + cheap gives up reliability, fast + reliable costs money, cheap + reliable is slow. Heroics only hide the bill until it arrives as outages or burnout.

first_principles.problem: Weekend crunches and skipped tests make it look like a team has all three. The debt comes due later as 3 a.m. outages, resignations or a predictable breach.
truths: People are not an infinite buffer.
derivation: **Fast + cheap** → reliability suffers (MVPs, hackathons).
**Fast + reliable** → cost rises (more engineers, redundancy, tooling).
**Cheap + reliable** → velocity drops (careful, slow change).
Recognise **heroics** as hidden debt.

analogy.title: Credit card spending
analogy.story: You can live beyond your means for a while on credit. The statement always comes, with interest.
analogy.breaks: Credit statements arrive on a known date. Engineering debt comes due unpredictably, often at the worst time.

example.title: The MVP that succeeded
example.scenario: A startup built fast and cheap; now it has real customers.

steps.label: Then
steps.detail: Manual SSH deploys, no monitoring: right for learning.

steps.label: Now
steps.detail: Customers pay, so the reliability bill must be paid.

example.outcome: the team sees today's outages as yesterday's conscious trade-off and budgets to repay it.

check.q: What does a fast and cheap approach usually sacrifice?

consciously-choosing-what-to-sacrifice.core: Don't try to balance the triangle evenly, which gives mediocrity everywhere. Lean deliberately into the two sides your business phase needs, write the choice down, and revisit it as the business changes.

first_principles.problem: Leaders who keep everything 'balanced' get a system that ships somewhat slowly, breaks somewhat often and costs somewhat too much, and nobody can explain why.
derivation: **Discovery**: velocity + cost, sacrifice reliability.
**Growth**: velocity + reliability, sacrifice cost.
**Maturity**: reliability + cost, sacrifice velocity.
**Document** the choice and **review** it quarterly.

analogy.title: Seasons on a farm
analogy.story: Spring is for planting fast, summer for protecting the crop, autumn for harvesting efficiently. A farmer who treats every season the same does badly in all.
analogy.breaks: Seasons change on schedule. Business phases don't, so watch signals (revenue, churn) to know when to shift.

example.title: Shifting from discovery to growth

steps.label: Decision
steps.detail: Hire an SRE, add multi-AZ and on-call.

steps.label: Record
steps.detail: Write it down so finance and product understand the higher bill.

example.outcome: spend and effort follow the business's real priorities.

check.q: What do you sacrifice in the growth phase, typically?
check.a: Cost: you spend more to keep velocity high and reliability good.

the-pressure-valve-feature-freezes-and-e.core: When velocity has starved reliability too long, error budgets give an objective trigger: if the SLO budget is spent, features pause and reliability work takes priority until it recovers.

first_principles.problem: Product wants features; on-call engineers are drowning in pages. Without a rule, the louder side wins and the system slides until velocity itself collapses under firefighting.
truths: Some unreliability is acceptable (100% is unaffordable).
Debt eventually slows feature work too.
derivation: Set an **SLO** (e.g. 99.9%) and its **error budget** (0.1% bad events).
While budget remains, **ship freely**.
When it's spent, **freeze features** and fix reliability.
Agree the policy **in advance** with product.

analogy.title: A household budget
analogy.story: You can spend on treats while there's money left this month. Once it's gone, spending stops until next month's income, whoever is asking.
analogy.breaks: Money is objective. Error budgets need good SLIs, or teams argue about the numbers instead.

example.title: A month of outages
example.scenario: The 99.9% SLO's monthly budget (43 minutes) is gone by day 12.

steps.label: Freeze
steps.detail: No feature deploys; only reliability fixes.

steps.label: Fix
steps.detail: Address the top two incident causes.

example.outcome: the reliability-vs-features argument is settled by data and a prior agreement.

check.q: How large is a monthly error budget for 99.9%?
check.a: About 43 minutes of downtime (0.1% of ~30 days).

the-iron-triangle-in-devops-and-platform.core: The triangle shows up in daily platform choices: pipeline depth, single vs multi-region, managed vs self-hosted, on-call design. Recognising it in the moment turns firefighting into deliberate engineering.

first_principles.problem: Engineers make dozens of small trade-offs a week (skip a test stage, add a region, self-host a tool) without noticing they're choosing a vertex.
truths: Every infra choice moves the triangle.
derivation: **CI/CD**: fast pipeline (skip integration tests) vs thorough (45 min) vs parallel (costly).
**Regions**: single (cheap, fragile), active-passive (middle), active-active (2–3× cost).
**Managed vs self-hosted**: pay money vs pay engineer time.

analogy.title: Packing for a trip
analogy.story: Every item you add (spare charger, umbrella) makes the trip safer but the bag heavier and slower. You choose item by item.
analogy.breaks: Packing happens once. Platforms evolve, so re-evaluate choices as scale changes.

example.title: Choosing multi-region
example.scenario: A team debates active-active for a B2B app with 99.9% SLO.
flow: SLO needs: minutes of failover OK

steps.label: Choice
steps.detail: Active-passive meets it at much lower cost.

example.outcome: the right resilience level is bought, not the maximum.

points: The triangle is in every infra choice.
Managed vs self-hosted is money vs time.

check.a: If the SLO tolerates minutes of failover, it meets requirements at far lower cost.
